props.title: My Name Is Joe
props.initialSlug: Reformed alcoholic faces challenges in Glasgow

sections.content: Ken Loach's My Name Is Joe (1998) stands as a masterpiece of British social realism, powered by Peter Mullan's raw, BAFTA-winning performance as a recovering alcoholic in Glasgow. The film follows the same unflinching tradition as Loach's Riff-Raff (1991) and Ladybird, Ladybird (1994), examining working-class struggles through an intensely personal lens. Mullan's Joe Kavanagh embodies the complex reality of addiction recovery while trying to build a relationship with health visitor Sarah (Louise Goodall), creating a love story that feels painfully authentic against Glasgow's harsh economic landscape.

sections.content: The film's examination of addiction recovery parallels other powerful British dramas like Naked (1993) and Trainspotting (1996), but Loach's documentary-style approach strips away any glamorization. The handheld camera work and use of local, often non-professional actors creates an authenticity that influenced later social realist works like Fish Tank (2009) and I, Daniel Blake (2016). The Glasgow dialect is left unvarnished, requiring subtitles for many viewers, but this linguistic authenticity is crucial to the film's impact.

What sets My Name Is Joe apart is its delicate balance between hope and despair. Unlike the bleaker Tyrannosaur (2011) or Dead Man's Shoes (2004), Loach allows moments of warmth and humor to punctuate the harsh reality. The football team Joe coaches becomes a symbol of community resilience, while his relationship with Sarah offers the possibility of redemption without guaranteeing it. This complex emotional palette influenced later British filmmakers like Shane Meadows and Andrea Arnold. SUBHEAD: The Legacy of British Social Realism

sections.content: My Name Is Joe builds on the tradition of British kitchen sink dramas like Saturday Night and Sunday Morning (1960) and Kes (1969), but updates their approach for the post-Thatcher era. The film's exploration of unemployment and community breakdown in Glasgow created a template for examining post-industrial Britain that later films like This Is England (2006) and The Full Monty (1997) would follow. Loach's commitment to showing working-class lives without sentimentality or condescension remains influential in contemporary British cinema.
